name: Sɛkpɛlé
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Delalorm, Cephas. 2016. Documentation and description of Sɛkpɛlé: a Ghana-Togo Mountain language of Ghana. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London. 660 pp. (open access: SOAS eprints 22780 / CORE 77066664; copy consulted downloaded from the Internet Archive the Internet Archive copy of CORE).
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'Sɛkpɛlé phonology', §3.2 'Tone and intonation', pp. 66-67; §3.3 'Syllable structures', p. 68.
catalog_quote: If the pitch on individual syllables brings about different meanings in words which are otherwise segmentally identical in a language, then that language is a tone language (Bodomo, 1997:13). There are two types of tones: register (level), and contour tones. Sɛkpɛlé has two register tones: high and low. Tones are used to contrast mono-syllabic words such as the following: 5) tó ‘throw’ tò ‘build’ 6) té ‘sell’ tè ‘know’ 7) ká ‘drive’ kà ‘insult’ ... Contour tones occur in cases where there are identical adjacent vowels differing only in tone, resulting in automatic lengthening for either a rising or falling tone ... There are two functions of tone: lexical and grammatical. The lexical function of tone applies to examples 5 to 8. Tone performs a grammatical function when a tone difference distinguishes grammatical categorises. Tone is used to distinguish TAM in Sɛkpɛlé ... Intonation involves the use of pitch variation in relation to an entire sentence rather than with syllables and words (Bodomo, 1997:13). ... Syllables bear tone in Sɛkpɛlé such that any segment that bears tone is capable of standing alone as a syllable or combines with other segments to form a syllabic structure.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sɛkpɛlé is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone on every syllable; contour tones arise from sequences of identical vowels with different tones. The source says nothing about word stress at all — no prominence rule, no claim that stress is absent — so there is no stress placement to record. (Ameka 2009 JWAL p. 141 instead reports three level tones H, M, L plus falling and rising, likewise without any stress statement.)
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only prosodic variation noted is dialectal: 'there seems to be some variation in terms of accent and style. Situnkpa seems to have some variant intonation' (p. 37, §1.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described on syllables and words (lexical contrast in monosyllables, grammatical contrast on subject-cross-reference prefixes); intonation is treated as sentence-level (rising H over the final word for questions).
new_statements.identity_note: Delalorm 2016 describes Sɛkpɛlé proper (the Situnkpa/Semate/Sela varieties of the Likpe traditional area), explicitly setting aside Sekwá (Bakwa, Todome) and Sɛlɛ/Santrokofi (Glottolog sele1249) as other members of the Sele continuum. Funke 1911, listed by Glottolog under sekp1241, is a description of Santrokofi (sele1249), not Sɛkpɛlé.

new_statements.quote: Die Tonbezeichnungen sind ebenfalls ganz unverändert gelassen. Man wird annehmen dürfen, daß es sich im wesentlichen um Tonhöhen handelt; der Akut bedeutet hohen, der Gravis tiefen Ton. Funke bezeichnet außerdem Mitteltöne, fallende und steigende Töne.
new_statements.translation: The tone markings have likewise been left entirely unchanged. One may assume that they essentially represent pitch levels; the acute denotes a high tone, the grave a low tone. Funke additionally marks mid tones, falling and rising tones.
new_statements.citation: Westermann, Diedrich. 1922. Vier Sprachen aus Mitteltogo: Likpe, Bowili, Akpafu und Adele. MSOS 25(3): 1-59.
new_statements.locator: Editorial preface, printed p. 2 of MSOS 1922 Abt. III (p. 172 of the archive.org scan); Likpe section = 'I. Likpe', printed pp. 3 ff. (pp. 173 ff.); Likpe-internal tone remarks at printed pp. 7, 9, 11 (pp. 177, 179, 181)

Man wird annehmen dürfen, daß es sich im wesentlichen um Tonhöhen handelt; der Akut bedeutet hohen, der Gravis tiefen Ton. Funke bezeichnet außerdem Mitteltöne, fallende und steigende Töne.' — verbatim. (Both scanned layers garble it — 'Tonbezeichimngen', 'unvei-ändert', 'düi'fen' — so a text a full-text search for stress/accent fails; the extracted text has it at lines 9397-9400, the djvu layer at 8573-8576.) Surrounding section = the ed…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Delalorm 2016 statement (Sɛkpɛlé is a tone language; no stress statement) and with Ameka 2009; it adds nothing about stress. Westermann's tone note is a remark on Funke's transcription of all his languages (Likpe, Bowili, Akpafu), not a Likpe-specific analysis; his H/L (+ Funke's mid, falling, rising) is consistent with Delalorm's two register tones H/L plus contour tones from vowel sequences and with Ameka's three-level H/M/L description. The catalog record's rule field is empty, so nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement on word stress at all. The article is a grammar sketch (gender, case, noun classes, pronouns, numerals, verb) plus wordlists compiled from Missionary E. Funke's field notes, with no Lautlehre/phonology section; a search of the whole article for betont/Betonung/Akzent/Nachdruck finds nothing (the only 'betont' hits are in the East-Asian part of the volume). The one prosodic statement is the compilers note that the tone marks in Funke's material (Likpe, Bowili, Akpafu) are pitch marks: acute = high, grave = low, plus mid, falling and rising tones. Inside the Likpe section tone is invoked three times in passing: the stem syllable -na of ethnonyms is 'tieftonig' (low-toned) (p. 7), the demonstrative namfo 'this/that' is distinguished 'mit verschiedenem Tonfall' (p. 9), and the ordinals show 'Tonverschiebungen' (tone shifts) (p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Likpe' is the Ewe exonym for Sɛkpɛlé (Glottolog sekp1241); the Likpe data come exclusively from Missionary Emil Funke's notes (article preface, p. 1). The same article also treats Bowili (= Tuwuli), Akpafu (= Siwu), Adele and the extinct Boro, which are separate GTM languages; the tone-mark note on p. 2 covers Funke's transcription of Likpe, Bowili and Akpafu jointly, and Mischlich's Adele/Boro material separately.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Sɛkpɛlé phonology' (pp. 60-73); §3.2 'Tone and intonation' pp. 66-68 (pp. 67-69): two register tones H and L with lexical and grammatical (TAM) function; falling/rising contours arise from adjacent identical vowels differing in tone; intonation (rising for questions) marked as H across the final word.
